name: Pioppi diet

card.summary: The Pioppi diet is a Mediterranean-inspired, low-carbohydrate, higher-fat eating plan from a 2017 book, aimed at weight and metabolic health that show up in body composition and skin and face leanness.
card.note: Dietitians' bodies have criticised its saturated-fat position; people with medical conditions usually consult a clinician before changing diet.

quick.overview:
The Pioppi diet comes from The Pioppi Diet: A 21-Day Lifestyle Plan (Penguin, 2017) by cardiologist Aseem Malhotra and Donal O'Neill. It is named after Pioppi, an Italian village associated with the Mediterranean diet.

People follow it for fat loss and leaner body composition, which changes how the body and face look, and for the metabolic health claims made for low-carb eating.
quick.how: The plan centres on olive oil, nuts, fibrous vegetables, low-sugar fruit and oily fish, avoids added sugar, refined carbohydrates (bread, pasta, rice) and seed oils, allows butter, cheese, dark chocolate and yoghurt, and caps red meat at 500 g a week.
quick.risks: The British Dietetic Association listed it among its 'top 5 worst celeb diets to avoid in 2018', the British Nutrition Foundation says it departs from a traditional Mediterranean diet, and the British Heart Foundation has called Malhotra's wider saturated-fat views misleading. Supporters say it is a lifestyle approach rather than a short diet.

lead: The Pioppi diet is a low-carbohydrate, higher-fat eating plan presented as a Mediterranean-style lifestyle. It was set out in The Pioppi Diet: A 21-Day Lifestyle Plan (Penguin Books, 2017) by British cardiologist Aseem Malhotra with Donal O'Neill. [1][2]

Followers use it to lose body fat and improve metabolic markers, which affects physique and facial leanness. The plan encourages extra-virgin olive oil, tree nuts, vegetables, oily fish and low-sugar fruit, while avoiding added sugar, refined carbohydrates and seed oils. [2]
The book was reviewed in the British Journal of General Practice, and its claims drew public criticism from dietitians. [1][2]

angle.text: People use the diet to reduce body fat. Because fat loss changes jaw, cheek and waist definition, it is used as a route to a leaner look.

paras: The book recommends 2-4 tablespoons of extra-virgin olive oil daily, a handful of nuts, 5-7 portions of fibrous vegetables and oily fish at least three times a week. It excludes added sugars, juice, refined flour foods and seed oils, allows dairy, butter, coconut oil and very dark chocolate, and permits alcohol within NHS limits. [2]
The authors argue that saturated fat can be eaten freely and call for policy change to address an environment that promotes obesity. [2]
The British Dietetic Association named it one of the 'top 5 worst celeb diets to avoid in 2018', describing it as a low-carb diet using the Mediterranean name. [2]

The British Nutrition Foundation says it conflicts with a traditional Mediterranean diet, which includes bread, pasta and rice and is typically low in saturated fat. The British Heart Foundation has called Malhotra's wider saturated-fat views misleading. [2]
No studies found testing the Pioppi diet as a package. The book was reviewed in the British Journal of General Practice in 2017. [1]

timeline.event: The Pioppi Diet: A 21-Day Lifestyle Plan is published by Penguin. [2]
British Dietetic Association lists it among diets to avoid. [2]
